fingerprint.event_title: Sommet de Genève : un accord historique sur le climat, mais critiqué par les ONG

synthesis_text: {"Numbers & Data": [{"text": "A total of 180 countries have signed a pact to reduce global carbon emissions by 50 percent by 2035, a goal that climate experts say is one of the most ambitious ever agreed at a multilateral forum.", "fact_indices": [0], "confirmation_count": 2}], "Exclusive / Single-Source": [{"text": "The 50 percent reduction is not a voluntary aspiration: the agreement includes trade sanctions for countries that fail to meet their commitments without technical justification, a novelty that has generated intense debate among delegates during the two weeks of negotiations.", "fact_indices": [1], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "\"This 100 billion reflects our conviction that the energy transition cannot wait, and that emerging nations deserve real support, not empty promises\". The Green Transition Fund will be used to finance renewable energy infrastructure, clean technology transfer, transport electrification and sustainable industrial conversion in countries that still rely on coal and fossil fuels for their economic development.", "fact_indices": [3], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "Climatologists at Oxford University and the Potsdam Research Institute have calculated that if fully implemented, the Geneva agreement could limit global warming to about 1.7 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, approaching the aspirational threshold of 1.5 degrees set in the Paris Agreement.", "fact_indices": [5], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "The 180 signatory countries have 18 months to ratify the agreement at national level and present their detailed implementation plans.", "fact_indices": [6], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "The first progress review is scheduled for the 2028 Climate Summit in Nairobi.As delegates leave Geneva, the message echoing in the hallways of the International Conference Centre is clear: the world has drawn a map for a decarbonised future, but the road is full of political, technological and financial obstacles that only collective will can overcome.", "fact_indices": [7], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "Financing: The Fund will be financed in a tripartite way: direct involvement of the industrialized countries (United States, European Union, Japan).", "fact_indices": [8], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "The final consensus hides deep geopolitical compromises: The flexibility clause: To get the signature of industrial superpowers and some emerging countries, a \"national flexibility\" clause was incorporated, allowing for adjustments to the intermediate reduction levels until 2030.", "fact_indices": [10], "confirmation_count": 1}], "Official Statements": [{"text": "Li Wei's announcement was met with a standing ovation by most delegates, and marks a turning point in China's participation in international climate finance. \"China is not only part of the problem, but also a fundamental force in building the solution\", Li Wei declared from the United Nations' rostrum.", "fact_indices": [2], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "\"It is a victory for climate justice, though smaller than expected\", said representatives of several African nations at a press conference after the closing ceremony.", "fact_indices": [4], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "This is an unprecedented step that will redefine our industrial trajectory for the next century, said US President Jane Smith at the closing session.", "fact_indices": [9], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "In a scathing statement, the organisation said:  The measures adopted in Geneva are largely inadequate and far too late.", "fact_indices": [11], "confirmation_count": 1}, {"text": "The final pact seals an unprecedented global commitment: to reduce carbon emissions by 50% by 2035 (compared to
